lesson.title: After Watergate: Ford, Carter, and the Search for Trust
lesson.summary: Gerald Ford and Jimmy Carter each came to the presidency promising to restore trust in government after Watergate, and each found that good intentions were not enough to solve the economic and foreign policy crises of the 1970s.
lesson.body:
Gerald Ford became president on August 9, 1974, the day Richard Nixon resigned in the wake of the Watergate scandal, and he remains the only person to serve as president without ever being elected to the presidency or the vice presidency. Ford had been appointed vice president in 1973 under the terms of the 25th Amendment after Nixon's original vice president, Spiro Agnew, resigned over an unrelated corruption case. Ford entered office promising that the nation's long national nightmare was over, but his presidency was shadowed almost immediately by his decision, on September 8, 1974, to grant Nixon a full pardon for any crimes he may have committed as president. Many Americans saw the pardon as proof that Washington still protected its own, and Ford's approval ratings never fully recovered.

Ford's presidency also had to manage the final collapse of the American position in Vietnam. In April 1975, North Vietnamese forces captured Saigon, ending the Vietnam War and the government of South Vietnam, and Ford oversaw the chaotic evacuation of American personnel and Vietnamese allies from the city. On the world stage, Ford signed the Helsinki Accords in 1975, an agreement with the Soviet Union and European nations that recognized existing European borders while committing signatories to respect human rights, a document that later gave Soviet dissidents a tool to hold their own government accountable. At home, Ford struggled to respond to rising inflation and unemployment, and his Whip Inflation Now campaign, built around WIN buttons, became a symbol of how limited the government's tools seemed against the economic problems of the decade.

Jimmy Carter, a former peanut farmer and governor of Georgia with little Washington experience, won the 1976 election by presenting himself as an outsider who could restore honesty to government after Watergate, defeating Ford in a close race. Carter's outsider status was an asset in 1976 but became a liability once he had to work with Congress, and he often struggled to build the political relationships needed to pass his agenda. Carter's clearest foreign policy achievement came in September 1978, when he brought Israeli Prime Minister Menachem Begin and Egyptian President Anwar Sadat together at Camp David and helped negotiate a framework for peace between the two countries, a breakthrough that led to a formal peace treaty in 1979. Carter also negotiated treaties in 1977 that would transfer control of the Panama Canal to Panama by the end of the century, a move that was popular abroad but controversial with conservatives at home.

Carter's presidency, like Ford's, was ultimately overwhelmed by problems that had roots deeper than either administration, especially the energy crisis and inflation of the 1970s, and the Iranian hostage crisis that began in late 1979. In July 1979, with his approval ratings falling and confidence in government still shaken by the legacy of Watergate, Carter delivered a televised address, often remembered as the malaise speech even though he never used that word, warning of a crisis of confidence threatening the country. Both Ford and Carter, in different ways, showed how difficult it was to govern in the years after Watergate, when public trust in the presidency itself had been badly damaged.
